fetched_contents.text: Chapter 7 Financial Inclusion in: Promoting Inclusive Growth in the Middle East and North Africa Introduction Financial inclusion, defined as the access to and use of formal financial services, is taking higher policy priority in many countries across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region as they face formidable challenges to achieving stronger and more inclusive growth and a more vibrant private sector.2 As stated in the 2018 Opportunity for All paper (Purfield and others 2018) and in Chapter 1 of this book, financial inclusion of both households and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in the MENA region lags that of other regions. The percentage of adults with an account in a formal financial institution—commonly referred to as the share of the “banked population”—is similar to that of the Caucasus and Central Asia (CCA) region but lower than in other regions, with the exception of sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The average share of SMEs in total bank lending in MENA countries is only about 9 percent, the lowest in the world. This chapter highlights the macroeconomic benefits of increasing financial inclusion in the MENA region, both in terms of growth and job creation. It also identifies the factors that can facilitate financial inclusion in the region and offers policy recommendations to expand financial inclusion. The chapter is organized as follows: the first section presents the state of financial inclusion in the MENA region. The second section discusses the macroeconomic benefits from increasing access to finance. The third section builds on recent empirical analyses (Barajas and others 2020; Fouejieu, Ndoye, and Sydorenko 2020) to identify key policies to increase access to and use of finance. The final section reviews the role of fintech and existing efforts in the MENA region to support financial inclusion. The State of Financial Inclusion in the MENA Region Households Based on the most recent data from the Global Findex Survey, in MENA countries the share of the banked population stood at 43 percent in 2017, compared with 52 percent for countries in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), 53 percent for Emerging and Developing Asia (EDA) countries, and 68 percent for Emerging and Developing Europe (EDE) countries (Figure 7.1, panel 1).3 On the other hand, this share is similar to that of CCA countries, and substantially greater than the 30 percent level registered in SSA countries. A similar pattern is visible for the percentage of adults who have either borrowed from a formal financial institution or who have used a credit card: at 14 percent, this is also well below the levels of LAC and EDE, while comparable to CCA and EDA and above that of SSA countries (Figure 7.1, panel 1). Furthermore, while about half of adult men are banked in MENA countries, only 37 percent of women are (Figure 7.1, panel 2). This divergence, of about 14 percentage points, is double the world average. There are also stark differences between two groups of countries within the MENA region. The high-income MENA countries have levels of account ownership and borrowing—77 and 33 percent, respectively—that exceed those in EDE, while in the other MENA countries, account ownership and borrowing are lower than in all regions except SSA. However, it is the high-income group that tends to display greater divergences in account holding according to age, income, work force participation and, particularly, level of education. In high-income MENA countries, an adult with at least a secondary education is 28 percentage points more likely to be banked than one with at most a primary education, compared to a 14 percentage point divergence in other MENA countries, and 23 points for the world as a whole, (Figure 7.1, panel 2). In recent years, MENA countries have shown progress in boosting account ownership but not so in use of credit by households. Between 2011 and 2017, account ownership increased by an average of 9 percentage points for MENA countries, while credit by households only increased in the high-income MENA countries (Figure 7.2, panel 1). The reasons for being “unbanked” largely mirror those in the rest of the world: the most common responses in the Global Findex Survey referred to not having sufficient funds (65 percent), to services being too expensive (28 percent), and to other family members having an account (26 percent), as in the rest of the world (Figure 7.2, panel 2). Small and Medium Enterprises SMEs (firms with fewer than 100 employees) represent about 97 percent of all registered companies in the MENA region and employ more than half of the total labor force, broadly in line with the world averages (Figure 7.3). A relatively large share of SMEs in the region are in the informal sector, creating a barrier for accessing formal credit channels. The MENA region lags other regions in terms of SME access to financing through the banking system. The share of SMEs’ bank lending is as low as 1.9 percent in Bahrain compared to 18 percent in Morocco (Figure 7.4, panel 2). It has also stagnated over the last 15 years in the MENA region (Figure 7.4, panel 3). Abstract Adoption of technology in the financial services industry (i.e. fintech) has been accelerating in recent years. To systematically and comprehensively assess the extent and progress over time in financial inclusion enabled by technology, we develop a novel digital financial inclusion index. This index is based on payments data covering 52 developing countries for 2014 and 2017, taking into account both access and usage dimentions of digital financial services (DFSs). This index is then combined with the traditional measures of financial inclusion in the literature and aggregated into an overall index of financial inlusion. There are two key findings: first, the adoption of fintech has been a key driver of financial inclusion. Second, there is wide variation across countries and regions, with the greatest progress recorded in Africa and Asia and the Pacific regions. This index should offer a useful analytical tool for researchers and policy makers. World Bank and IMF databases differ in how they define and operationalize financial inclusion, with the World Bank emphasizing a broad demand-side survey approach and the IMF framing financial inclusion more narrowly around access and use of formal financial services.

On definitions, the World Bank’s Global Findex is described as the world’s only demand-side survey on financial inclusion and a leading source of data on how adults around the world access financial services [N1-F1]. The World Bank’s broader financial inclusion page also highlights that financial inclusion includes digital payments, savings, and borrowing behaviors across economies [N1-R2]. In contrast, the IMF chapter on financial inclusion defines it as “access to and use of formal financial services” and places it in the context of policy priority and inclusive growth [N2-R1]. The IMF’s Financial Access Survey (FAS) also uses indicators that are explicitly tied to formal financial institutions, including microfinance institutions, commercial banks, credit unions, and credit cooperatives [N2-R4]. This makes the IMF approach more institutionally centered, while the World Bank’s approach is more behaviorally centered.

On dimensions, the World Bank’s database emphasizes a wide range of adult behaviors, including account ownership, usage, and service access, and it provides over 800 country-level indicators summarized for all adults and disaggregated by key dimensions [N1-R1]. The IMF, by contrast, focuses on access and use of formal financial services and, through its FAS and related work, also measures usage in the context of SMEs and other formal financial institutions [N2-F2]. The IMF working paper further notes that traditional financial inclusion is measured by indicators related to access to and/or usage of traditional financial services, such as bank accounts per capita and ATM per capita, and that some recent studies quantify digital financial inclusion through mobile money accounts and financial transactions using mobile phones [N3-F3]. So the IMF places more emphasis on formal institutional access and usage, while the World Bank’s Global Findex includes broader behavioral and digital dimensions.

On accounts, usage, and services, the World Bank’s Global Findex database is demand-side, meaning it measures what adults actually do with financial services rather than only institutional provision [N1-F1]. It therefore captures account ownership, usage, and service access as part of a single demand-side perspective [N1-R4]. The IMF, by contrast, relies on survey-based measures of access and use of formal financial services, with the FAS explicitly measuring the percentage of adults with accounts in formal financial institutions and usage indicators such as borrowing or credit card use [N2-F2]. The IMF also uses firm-level data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey to construct a composite SME financial inclusion index, combining access and usage indicators [N2-F2]. This indicates that the IMF often aggregates access and usage into composite measures, while the World Bank’s Findex is more explicit about disaggregation by adult behavior.

On composite versus single-item indicators, the World Bank’s approach is clearly composite. The Global Findex is described as providing over 800 country-level indicators, implying a highly disaggregated and composite system of indicators rather than a single-item measure [N1-R1]. The IMF’s approach is similarly composite but is organized around formal institutional access and usage, with the FAS and related indicators used together to assess financial inclusion [N2-F2]. The IMF’s working paper also explicitly combines traditional financial inclusion measures with digital financial inclusion measures into an overall index, showing a composite construction strategy [N3-F3]. In short, both databases use composite indicators, but the World Bank’s composite system is broader and more behaviorally diverse, while the IMF’s composite system is more focused on formal access and usage across institutions and surveys.

Overall, the World Bank defines financial inclusion as a broad demand-side phenomenon covering adult access, usage, and service behavior, while the IMF defines it more narrowly as access to and use of formal financial services and often uses survey-based indicators tied to formal institutions [N1-R2][N2-R1]. The World Bank’s indicators are more disaggregated and composite, whereas the IMF’s are more institutionally focused and often aggregated into composite indices [N1-R1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

## Integrated final answer: How the World Bank and IMF databases differ in measuring financial inclusion

The World Bank and IMF databases differ in their approaches to measuring financial inclusion in three main ways: **how they define and operationalize financial inclusion**, **how they handle data sources and aggregation**, and **how they are organized in terms of coverage, accessibility, and institutional purpose**. The World Bank’s approach is broader, demand-side, and more survey-driven, while the IMF’s approach is more institutionally focused, survey-based, and often built around formal access and usage indicators.

### 1) Definition and operationalization

The World Bank defines financial inclusion through its **Global Findex database**, described as the world’s only **demand-side survey on financial inclusion** and a leading source of data on how adults around the world access financial services [N1-F1]. Its broader definition includes **digital payments, savings, and borrowing behaviors** across economies [N1-R2], and it provides over **800 country-level indicators** summarized for all adults and disaggregated by key dimensions [N1-R1]. This makes the World Bank’s definition highly behavioral and broad, covering adult access, usage, and service behavior across a wide set of dimensions.

By contrast, the IMF defines financial inclusion more narrowly as **“access to and use of formal financial services”** and frames it as a policy priority in many countries [N2-R1]. The IMF’s Financial Access Survey (FAS) is explicitly tied to formal financial institutions, including **microfinance institutions, commercial banks, credit unions, and credit cooperatives** [N2-R4]. The IMF’s approach is therefore more institutionally centered and narrower in scope, with a stronger emphasis on formal access and formal usage.

Both databases use composite indicators. The World Bank’s Global Findex is clearly composite, with hundreds of country-level indicators [N1-R1]. The IMF also uses composite indicators, including the G20 Financial Inclusion Indicators framework and the SME financial inclusion index built from firm-level data on access and usage [N2-F2]. The IMF’s working paper further shows that it combines **traditional financial inclusion measures** with **digital financial inclusion measures** into an overall index [N3-F3]. So both databases are composite, but the World Bank’s composite system is broader and more behaviorally diverse, while the IMF’s composite system is more focused on formal access and usage.

### 2) Data sources, aggregation, and harmonization

Methodologically, the World Bank relies heavily on its own **Global Findex survey** and related demand-side data [N1-F1]. Its database is described as the world’s only demand-side survey on financial inclusion, which means it is built around what adults actually do with financial services rather than only on institutional provision [N1-F1]. This survey basis shapes its aggregation: it provides **over 800 country-level indicators** and allows users to define custom aggregates using rules such as mean, median, sum, weighted mean, and so on [N1-F1].

The IMF’s methodological approach is also survey-based but more externally harmonized. The IMF’s **Financial Access Survey (FAS)** is explicitly used in studies and reports on financial inclusion [N2-R2], and the IMF working paper states that data on various dimensions of financial inclusion are compiled using global data sources including the IMF’s FAS and the World Bank [N3-R3]. The IMF’s G20 Financial Inclusion Indicators methodology note also says the GPFI database includes the **World Bank’s Enterprise Surveys** and the **IMF’s Financial Access Survey** [N3-R5]. This indicates that the IMF actively harmonizes financial inclusion indicators with other surveys, while the World Bank’s harmonization is more about user-level customization and aggregation within its own database [N1-F1][N3-R3][N3-R5].

In terms of aggregation, both databases produce composite indicators. The World Bank does so through a highly disaggregated demand-side survey system [N1-R1], while the IMF aggregates formal access and usage indicators into composite indices and sometimes combines them with digital measures [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The IMF’s working paper explicitly combines traditional and digital measures into an overall index, showing a deliberate composite aggregation strategy [N3-F3]. The World Bank’s system, by contrast, is more about producing a large set of indicators rather than a single composite score.

### 3) Coverage, timeliness, and accessibility

On coverage, the World Bank appears to have broader geographic reach. The Global Findex database is described as covering **148 economies**, including both high-income economies and developing (low- and middle-income) economies [N1-R5]. The evidence also suggests broad country engagement and country-level indicators [N1-R2]. The IMF evidence is thinner on specific country coverage, but it clearly focuses on **formal financial services and institutional access**, as reflected in its FAS and G20 indicators [N2-R2][N2-R3]. Because the IMF evidence does not provide a direct country-count figure, the comparison here is less precise, but the implication is that the IMF’s coverage is narrower and more institutionally focused than the World Bank’s broad adult-level survey coverage [N1-R5].

On timeliness and update frequency, the World Bank’s evidence suggests a regular update cycle, with the Findex database described as a leading source and the 2025 edition explicitly named in the evidence [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The IMF evidence is less explicit on update frequency, but the IMF chapter notes that the chapter draws on the **most recent data from the Global Findex Survey as of 2017**, indicating that the IMF’s own reports and analyses are built on the latest available survey data rather than on a fixed publication schedule [N2-F2]. This suggests that the IMF’s financial inclusion data are not self-contained in the evidence provided and that their use is tied to the World Bank’s Findex and other surveys, making frequency less transparent here [N2-F2].

On accessibility, the World Bank provides a more user-friendly interface. The Global Findex database in DataBank allows users to select countries, create custom groups, and define custom indicators using aggregation rules such as **weighted mean, mean, median, sum**, etc. [N1-F1]. This makes it relatively accessible for analysts and researchers. The IMF evidence here does not describe an equally accessible public interface in the same detail, and the only direct accessibility clue is that the IMF’s FAS data are used in reports and studies, suggesting a more specialized and less publicly exposed data portal than the World Bank’s DataBank [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In short, the World Bank’s system is more accessible for standard users, while the IMF’s data seem more accessible through reports and institutional analysis rather than through a direct public database interface [N1-F1][N2-R2].

### 4) Institutional role and intended audience

The World Bank’s mission is broad and demand-side. Its financial inclusion page describes inclusive finance as driving growth and resilience and notes that **1.4 billion adults globally remain unbanked** [N1-R2]. The World Bank’s mission also includes digital financial services and country engagement, which implies that its data are intended to support policy, research, and operational work across a wide audience [N1-R2][N4-R3]. Its database is therefore aimed at a broad audience of researchers, policymakers, and practitioners who need country-level, adult-level, and disaggregated financial inclusion data [N1-R1][N1-R2].

The IMF’s mission is more policy and macroeconomic. The IMF chapter on financial inclusion describes financial inclusion as **“access to and use of formal financial services”** and frames it as a key policy priority in many countries, especially in the Middle East and North Africa [N2-R1]. The IMF also emphasizes macroeconomic benefits, growth, and job creation, and it uses financial inclusion data in the context of SME access to finance and policy recommendations [N2-F2]. The IMF’s audience is therefore narrower but still broad, with a strong emphasis on analysts, policymakers, and institutions that need evidence for policy decisions [N2-F2][N2-R2].

### 5) Governance and validation processes

Governance and validation differ as well. On dimensions, the World Bank’s database emphasizes a wide range of adult behaviors, including account ownership, usage, and service access, and it provides over 800 country-level indicators summarized for all adults and disaggregated by key dimensions [N1-R1]. The IMF, by contrast, focuses on access and use of formal financial services and, through its FAS and related work, also measures usage in the context of SMEs and other formal financial institutions [N2-F2]. ## Integrated final answer: How the World Bank and IMF databases differ in measuring financial inclusion

The World Bank and IMF databases differ in their approaches to measuring financial inclusion in three main ways: **how they define and operationalize financial inclusion**, **how they handle data sources and aggregation**, and **how they are organized in terms of coverage, accessibility, and institutional purpose**. The World Bank’s approach is broader, demand-side, and more survey-driven, while the IMF’s approach is more institutionally focused, survey-based, and often built around formal access and usage indicators.

### 1) Definition and operationalization

The World Bank defines financial inclusion through its **Global Findex database**, described as the world’s only **demand-side survey on financial inclusion** and a leading source of data on how adults around the world access financial services [N1-F1]. Its broader definition includes **digital payments, savings, and borrowing behaviors** across economies [N1-R2], and it provides over **800 country-level indicators** summarized for all adults and disaggregated by key dimensions [N1-R1]. This makes the World Bank’s definition highly behavioral and broad, covering adult access, usage, and service behavior across a wide set of dimensions.

By contrast, the IMF defines financial inclusion more narrowly as **“access to and use of formal financial services”** and frames it as a policy priority in many countries [N2-R1]. The IMF’s Financial Access Survey (FAS) is explicitly tied to formal financial institutions, including **microfinance institutions, commercial banks, credit unions, and credit cooperatives** [N2-R4]. The IMF’s approach is therefore more institutionally centered and narrower in scope, with a stronger emphasis on formal access and formal usage.

Both databases use composite indicators. The World Bank’s Global Findex is clearly composite, with hundreds of country-level indicators [N1-R1]. The IMF also uses composite indicators, including the G20 Financial Inclusion Indicators framework and the SME financial inclusion index built from firm-level data on access and usage [N2-F2]. The IMF’s working paper further shows that it combines **traditional financial inclusion measures** with **digital financial inclusion measures** into an overall index [N3-F3]. So both databases are composite, but the World Bank’s composite system is broader and more behaviorally diverse, while the IMF’s composite system is more focused on formal access and usage.

### 2) Data sources, aggregation, and harmonization

Methodologically, the World Bank relies heavily on its own **Global Findex survey** and related demand-side data [N1-F1]. Its database is described as the world’s only demand-side survey on financial inclusion, which means it is built around what adults actually do with financial services rather than only on institutional provision [N1-F1]. This survey basis shapes its aggregation: it provides **over 800 country-level indicators** and allows users to define custom aggregates using rules such as mean, median, sum, weighted mean, and so on [N1-F1].

The IMF’s methodological approach is also survey-based but more externally harmonized. The IMF’s **Financial Access Survey (FAS)** is explicitly used in studies and reports on financial inclusion [N2-R2], and the IMF working paper states that data on various dimensions of financial inclusion are compiled using global data sources including the IMF’s FAS and the World Bank [N3-R3]. The IMF’s G20 Financial Inclusion Indicators methodology note also says the GPFI database includes the **World Bank’s Enterprise Surveys** and the **IMF’s Financial Access Survey** [N3-R5]. This indicates that the IMF actively harmonizes financial inclusion indicators with other surveys, while the World Bank’s harmonization is more about user-level customization and aggregation within its own database [N1-F1][N3-R3][N3-R5].

In terms of aggregation, both databases produce composite indicators. The World Bank does so through a highly disaggregated demand-side survey system [N1-R1], while the IMF aggregates formal access and usage indicators into composite indices and sometimes combines them with digital measures [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The IMF’s working paper explicitly combines traditional and digital measures into an overall index, showing a deliberate composite aggregation strategy [N3-F3]. The World Bank’s system, by contrast, is more about producing a large set of indicators rather than a single composite score.

### 3) Coverage, timeliness, and accessibility

On coverage, the World Bank appears to have broader geographic reach. The Global Findex database is described as covering **148 economies**, including both high-income economies and developing (low- and middle-income) economies [N1-R5]. The evidence also suggests broad country engagement and country-level indicators [N1-R2]. The IMF evidence is thinner on specific country coverage, but it clearly focuses on **formal financial services and institutional access**, as reflected in its FAS and G20 indicators [N2-R2][N2-R3]. Because the IMF evidence does not provide a direct country-count figure, the comparison here is less precise, but the implication is that the IMF’s coverage is narrower and more institutionally focused than the World Bank’s broad adult-level survey coverage [N1-R5].

On timeliness and update frequency, the World Bank’s evidence suggests a regular update cycle, with the Findex database described as a leading source and the 2025 edition explicitly named in the evidence [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The IMF evidence is less explicit on update frequency, but the IMF chapter notes that the chapter draws on the **most recent data from the Global Findex Survey as of 2017**, indicating that the IMF’s own reports and analyses are built on the latest available survey data rather than on a fixed publication schedule [N2-F2]. This suggests that the IMF’s financial inclusion data are not self-contained in the evidence provided and that their use is tied to the World Bank’s Findex and other surveys, making frequency less transparent here [N2-F2].

On accessibility, the World Bank provides a more user-friendly interface. The Global Findex database in DataBank allows users to select countries, create custom groups, and define custom indicators using aggregation rules such as **weighted mean, mean, median, sum**, etc. [N1-F1]. This makes it relatively accessible for analysts and researchers. The IMF evidence here does not describe an equally accessible public interface in the same detail, and the only direct accessibility clue is that the IMF’s FAS data are used in reports and studies, suggesting a more specialized and less publicly exposed data portal than the World Bank’s DataBank [N2-R2][N2-R4]. In short, the World Bank’s system is more accessible for standard users, while the IMF’s data seem more accessible through reports and institutional analysis rather than through a direct public database interface [N1-F1][N2-R2].

### 4) Institutional role and intended audience

The World Bank’s mission is broad and demand-side. Its financial inclusion page describes inclusive finance as driving growth and resilience and notes that **1.4 billion adults globally remain unbanked** [N1-R2]. The World Bank’s mission also includes digital financial services and country engagement, which implies that its data are intended to support policy, research, and operational work across a wide audience [N1-R2][N4-R3]. Its database is therefore aimed at a broad audience of researchers, policymakers, and practitioners who need country-level, adult-level, and disaggregated financial inclusion data [N1-R1][N1-R2].

The IMF’s mission is more policy and macroeconomic. The IMF chapter on financial inclusion describes financial inclusion as **“access to and use of formal financial services”** and frames it as a key policy priority in many countries, especially in the Middle East and North Africa [N2-R1]. The IMF also emphasizes macroeconomic benefits, growth, and job creation, and it uses financial inclusion data in the context of SME access to finance and policy recommendations [N2-F2]. The IMF’s audience is therefore narrower but still broad, with a strong emphasis on analysts, policymakers, and institutions that need evidence for policy decisions [N2-F2][N2-R2].

### 5) Governance and validation processes

Governance and validation differ as well. The World Bank’s system is presented as a public database with a transparent DataBank interface, allowing users to create custom indicators and apply aggregation rules [N1-F1]. The evidence does not explicitly describe a detailed validation process, but the public and customizable nature of the database implies a governance model that is accessible and user-facing [N1-F1]. The IMF’s evidence suggests a more institutionally embedded validation process: the IMF chapter draws on the most recent Global Findex Survey data as of 2017 and references firm-level data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey, indicating that IMF analyses are validated through survey-based evidence and external datasets [N2-F2]. The IMF working paper also explicitly states that its index is built on payments data and combines traditional and digital measures, showing a more methodologically explicit validation process than is visible in the World Bank’s evidence here [N3-F3]. In short, the IMF appears to validate its financial inclusion measures through survey data and external datasets, while the World Bank’s validation is implied through its public survey design and database accessibility [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

### Bottom line

The World Bank and IMF databases differ in a systematic way:

- **Definition**: The World Bank is broad and demand-side, while the IMF is narrower and institutionally focused [N1-F1][N2-R1].
- **Operationalization**: The World Bank emphasizes adult access, usage, and service behavior; the IMF emphasizes access and use of formal financial services and often aggregates access and usage into composite indices [N1-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2].
- **Sources**: The World Bank relies heavily on its own Global Findex survey; the IMF relies on its own FAS and often integrates external sources such as the World Bank’s Enterprise Survey [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5].
- **Aggregation**: Both databases produce composite indicators, but the World Bank does so through a highly disaggregated demand-side system, while the IMF aggregates formal access and usage indicators into composite indices and sometimes combines them with digital measures [N1-R1][N2-F2][N3-F3].
- **Coverage**: The World Bank has broader country coverage; the IMF evidence here suggests narrower, institutionally focused coverage [N1-R5].
- **Accessibility**: The World Bank is more accessible through DataBank; the IMF is more accessible through reports and analyses rather than a direct public interface [N1-F1][N2-R2].
- **Mission and audience**: The World Bank targets a broad audience for inclusive finance and digital access; the IMF targets analysts and policymakers focused on policy-relevant financial inclusion outcomes [N1-R2][N2-R1].
- **Governance and validation**: The IMF’s validation process is more explicitly tied to survey data and external datasets; the World Bank’s validation is implied through its public survey design and database accessibility [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

In short, the World Bank’s Global Findex is the broader, more accessible, and more behaviorally rich system, while the IMF’s financial inclusion data are more institutionally focused, survey-based, and often built around formal access and usage indicators [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-F2].
